etiologicalMechanism: PTSD is characterized by tonic hyperarousal, fragmented sleep architecture, and heightened threat processing that destabilize sleep-wake regulation and reduce arousal-threshold stability, promoting upper-airway collapse during sleep. Plausible shared and mediating pathways include PTSD-associated weight gain (obesity is a recognized risk factor but the corpus explicitly declines to treat an obesity-intermediate chain as established without veteran-specific evidence), sedative-hypnotic and antipsychotic medication effects, alcohol and tobacco use, and reduced physical activity; conversely, OSA-driven intermittent hypoxemia and sleep fragmentation amplify PTSD symptoms, producing a bidirectional relationship. Meta-analytic data from 12 studies found pooled OSA prevalence in PTSD of 75.7% (95% CI 44.1-92.5; AHI ≥ 5) and 43.6% (95% CI 20.6-69.7; AHI ≥ 10), with significantly higher prevalence in veterans than in non-veteran or mixed samples, and PTSD patients showed significantly lower CPAP adherence. A systematic review similarly found increased OSA prevalence in PTSD and major depression with considerable heterogeneity. In a cohort of 17,570 service members followed a median 8.4 years, PTSD independently predicted incident OSA (adjusted HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.46) after adjustment for TBI, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and obesity (obesity HR 2.40). Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a)-(b), direct causation or aggravation may be pleaded, but the population evidence supports association, not individual causation; the registered CRG edge is authored ASSOCIATION_ONLY. A nexus opinion requires polysomnography-confirmed OSA, chronology relative to PTSD onset/severity, weight and medication history, and exclusion of anatomic and lifestyle risk factors.

medicalEvidence.title: Prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea in patients with posttraumatic stress disorder and its impact on adherence to continuous positive airway pressure therapy: a meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Zhang Y, Weed J, Ren R, Tang X, Zhang W
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 12 studies: pooled OSA prevalence in PTSD 75.7% (AHI ≥ 5; 95% CI 44.1-92.5) and 43.6% (AHI ≥ 10; 95% CI 20.6-69.7); prevalence significantly higher in veterans, and PTSD patients had significantly poorer CPAP adherence.

medicalEvidence.title: Obstructive sleep apnea and psychiatric disorders: a systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Gupta MA, Simpson FC
medicalEvidence.summary: PRISMA systematic review (47 records) examining OSA prevalence in psychiatric populations: evidence suggests increased OSA prevalence in major depressive disorder and PTSD, with considerable heterogeneity across studies; reviews treatment considerations including CPAP adherence.

medicalEvidence.title: Obstructive sleep apnea among survivors of combat-related traumatic injury: a retrospective cohort study
medicalEvidence.authors: Haynes ZA, Stewart IJ, Poltavskiy E, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective cohort of 17,570 service members (median 8.4-year follow-up): PTSD predicted incident OSA (adjusted HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.46) independent of TBI (HR 1.39), depression (HR 1.52), anxiety (HR 1.40), insomnia (HR 1.71), and obesity (HR 2.40) — establishing both a PTSD signal and the dominant competing risk factor.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6847 (sleep apnea syndromes — obstructive, central, mixed)

primaryCondition: Service-connected knee osteoarthritis on chronic NSAID therapy
etiologicalMechanism: NSAIDs injure the upper gastrointestinal tract through two complementary mechanisms. Systemically, COX-1 (and COX-2) inhibition depletes prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) that maintain mucosal blood flow, mucus/bicarbonate secretion, epithelial repair, and immunoregulation, leaving the esophageal and gastroduodenal mucosa vulnerable to acid and pepsin; topically, prolonged tablet contact with esophageal mucosa — especially at anatomic narrowings and with recumbent dosing or inadequate fluid — causes chemical ('pill') esophagitis. A review of more than 650 published drug-induced esophagitis cases classified 21.8% as NSAID-associated injury aggravated by coexisting reflux, and meta-analytic data from 460,984 subjects found NSAID/aspirin use associated with reflux symptoms (OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.10-1.88). A representative national survey of 6,823 French adults found GERD symptoms significantly more common among NSAID users (27% vs 19%, P ≤ 0.001), with NSAID use remaining an independent predictor after logistic regression. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately resulting from treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so documented chronic NSAID therapy for service-connected osteoarthritis can support GERD as a secondary medication-effect claim — the theory the corpus already applies to the analogous rheumatoid-arthritis→GERD edge. Critical limits: NSAIDs are more strongly associated with dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease than with GERD per se; dyspepsia is not GERD, and ulcer/gastritis must be rated under its own diagnostic codes. A nexus opinion must document drug, dose, and duration; GERD diagnosis (not symptom overlap); and exclusion of hiatal hernia, obesity, smoking, alcohol, H. pylori, and other reflux causes.

medicalEvidence.title: Global prevalence of, and risk factors for, gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms: a meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Eusebi LH, Ratnakumaran R, Yuan Y, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis of 108 populations (460,984 subjects): pooled weekly GORD symptom prevalence 13.3% (95% CI 12.0-14.6). NSAID/aspirin use was associated with reflux symptoms (OR 1.44; 95% CI 1.10-1.88), alongside age ≥50, smoking, and obesity.

medicalEvidence.title: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use as a risk factor for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: an observational study
medicalEvidence.authors: Ruszniewski P, Soufflet C, Barthélémy P
medicalEvidence.summary: National survey of 6,823 evaluable French adults: 33% reported NSAID use in the prior 3 months; GERD symptoms were significantly more common in NSAID users (27% vs 19%, P ≤ 0.001), and NSAID use was an independent predictor of reflux symptoms on logistic regression.

medicalEvidence.title: Drug-induced esophagitis
medicalEvidence.authors: Zografos GN, Georgiadou D, Thomas D, Kaltsas G, Digalakis M
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of >650 reported drug-induced esophagitis cases from 30+ medications. NSAID-associated injury accounted for 21.8% of the persistent-esophagitis group, with injury aggravated by coexisting gastroesophageal reflux; lesions predominate at anatomic narrowings (75.6% middle third).

medicalEvidence.title: Prostaglandins, NSAIDs, and gastric mucosal protection: why doesn't the stomach digest itself?
medicalEvidence.authors: Wallace JL
medicalEvidence.summary: Mechanistic review establishing that prostaglandin synthesis blockade by NSAIDs impairs essentially every component of mucosal defense and repair, explaining increased susceptibility to injury and impaired ulcer healing with chronic NSAID ingestion.

medicalEvidence.title: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) Induced Dyspepsia
medicalEvidence.authors: Yap PR, Goh KL
medicalEvidence.summary: Review clarifying that NSAIDs significantly increase dyspepsia risk, that dyspepsia correlates poorly with underlying ulceration, and that erosive esophagitis may contribute — an important caution against equating NSAID dyspepsia with a GERD diagnosis.

38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7206 (GERD; evaluated under DC 7203 criteria)
38 CFR § 4.114, DC 7203 (esophagitis/stricture) and DC 7346 (hiatal hernia) where applicable

etiologicalMechanism: Chronic subjective tinnitus is sustained by maladaptive central auditory plasticity — reduced inhibition and increased spontaneous firing in the dorsal cochlear nucleus and auditory cortex — amplified by limbic/attentional networks and by comorbid sleep disruption. Migraine is a trigeminovascular disorder with cortical hyperexcitability and impaired sensory habituation; trigeminal activation releases CGRP and can modulate auditory-cortex gain, and clinical observation shows that migraine attacks can change tinnitus loudness in some patients, while up to 45% of tinnitus patients report comorbid migraine. Population evidence is strongest in the direction migraine→tinnitus (a systematic review of 26,166 participants found high odds/hazard ratios for migraine as a tinnitus-associated condition), so the defensible secondary theory is aggravation of an already-documented migraine baseline by service-connected tinnitus: continuous aversive auditory input, tinnitus-related distress, and sleep fragmentation act as nonspecific triggers that lower the trigeminovascular activation threshold and increase attack frequency and severity. A prospective study of 286 clinically examined tinnitus patients found 49.3% met ICHD-3 criteria for a headache disorder (mostly tension-type or migraine), with 58.16% reporting identical localization of tinnitus and head pain — supporting shared central pathophysiology rather than coincidence. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(b), aggravation requires a documented baseline migraine disorder worsened beyond its expected course; de novo causation of migraine by tinnitus is not established by longitudinal evidence. Because the association is bidirectional and confounded by insomnia, medication-overuse headache, cervicalgia, and stress, a nexus opinion must address chronology, headache diaries before and after tinnitus onset/severity change, and alternative etiologies.

medicalEvidence.title: Migraine associated with tinnitus and hearing loss in adults: a systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Campello CP, Lemos C, Andrade W, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: PROSPERO-registered systematic review of 6 observational studies (26,166 participants). Most studies showed an association between migraine and tinnitus, with high odds and hazard ratios for tinnitus among migraineurs; migraine was present in 10.1% and 22.5% of tinnitus patients in two investigations.

medicalEvidence.title: The Prevalence of Different Types of Headache in Patients with Subjective Tinnitus and Its Influence on Tinnitus Parameters: A Prospective Clinical Study
medicalEvidence.authors: Nowaczewska M, Wiciński M, Straburzyński M, Kaźmierczak W
medicalEvidence.summary: Prospective study of 286 patients with subjective non-pulsating tinnitus; 141 (49.3%) were diagnosed with headache (mostly tension-type or migraine), and 58.16% reported the same localization of tinnitus and headache. Higher tinnitus burden (THI), younger age, female sex, and hearing loss were independently associated with headache.

medicalEvidence.title: A proposed association between subjective nonpulsatile tinnitus and migraine
medicalEvidence.authors: Lee A, Abouzari M, Akbarpour M, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Narrative review proposing shared central mechanisms: up to 45% of tinnitus patients have comorbid migraine; trigeminal nerve activation of the auditory cortex during attacks and increased vascular permeability are hypothesized to exacerbate tinnitus. Notes promising responses of tinnitus to migraine therapies.

medicalEvidence.title: Low Evidence for Tinnitus Risk Factors: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Biswas R, Genitsaridi E, Trpchevska N, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review restricted to cohort/case-control designs (49 studies screened, 25 with usable estimates). Found little robust evidence for causal risk factors beyond hearing-related exposures — an important ceiling on causation claims for tinnitus pathways.

secondaryDiagnosticCode: 8520 (38 CFR § 4.124a; neuralgic presentations may rate under the corresponding neuralgia code)
primaryCondition: Degenerative disc disease / intervertebral disc syndrome
etiologicalMechanism: Degenerative disc disease progresses from proteoglycan loss and annular tears to disc herniation, endplate changes, and osteophyte formation, narrowing the central canal, lateral recess, or neural foramen. The extruded nucleus pulposus compresses the nerve root and releases inflammatory mediators — TNF-alpha, IL-6, phospholipase A2, nitric oxide, and prostaglandins — producing mechanical and chemical radicular irritation, with dermatomal pain and paresthesias, myotomal weakness, and diminished reflexes. The VA rating schedule itself embodies this causal link: DC 5243 (intervertebral disc syndrome) is assignable only when there is 'disc herniation with compression and/or irritation of the adjacent nerve root.' A NASS evidence-based clinical guideline defines the diagnostic standard for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy, and a Cochrane review establishes the performance limits of physical examination (including straight-leg raise) against imaging for identifying disc-related radiculopathy. A systematic review of 59 studies quantified incidence, with annual estimates ranging from 0.3-2.7 per 1,000 persons (surgical case definitions) to 0.04-1.5 per 1,000 (hospital-based definitions). Spontaneous regression of herniated disc material is well documented and frequently improves symptoms, so a nexus opinion must show persistent, anatomically concordant radicular impairment. Adjudication caution: under § 4.71a the 5242/5243 evaluation may already compensate radicular signs, and a separate DC 8520 rating risks pyramiding — rate the predominant disability picture. Registry note: the existing CRG edge is restricted to anatomically concordant cervical nerve-root disease (ME-13, citing Alomar 2022); this lumbar mapping is a scope extension requiring the same bounded-proposition discipline. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), the causal mechanism is among the best-established on this list, but individual claims still require concordant imaging, electrodiagnostic or exam findings, and exclusion of peripheral entrapment, plexopathy, and nondegenerative structural lesions.

medicalEvidence.title: Incidence of and risk factors for lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy in adults: a systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Hincapié CA, Kroismayr D, Hofstetter L, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review (87 studies reviewed; 59 synthesized; best-evidence synthesis of low/moderate risk-of-bias studies): annual incidence of LDH with radiculopathy ranged from 0.3-2.7 per 1,000 (surgical definitions) to 0.04-1.5 per 1,000 (hospital-based definitions), with risk-factor synthesis supporting a multifactorial model.

medicalEvidence.title: An evidence-based clinical guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: Kreiner DS, Hwang SW, Easa JE, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: North American Spine Society evidence-based clinical guideline establishing contemporary diagnostic and treatment standards for symptomatic lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy — the standard-of-care reference for the clinical nexus between disc pathology and radicular impairment.

medicalEvidence.title: Physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy due to disc herniation in patients with low-back pain
medicalEvidence.authors: van der Windt DA, Simons E, Riphagen II, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review: assesses how physical examination tests identify radiculopathy due to lower lumbar disc herniation in patients with low-back pain and sciatica; most patients respond to conservative treatment, and imaging correlation remains essential for surgical selection.

medicalEvidence.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of predictive factors for spontaneous regression in lumbar disc herniation
medicalEvidence.authors: Rashed S, Vassiliou A, Starup-Hansen J, Tsang K
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis confirming spontaneous regression of lumbar disc herniation is well documented and synthesizing predictors by disc morphology — a prognosis counterweight requiring nexus opinions to demonstrate persistent rather than transient radicular findings.

38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8520 (paralysis of the sciatic nerve)

secondaryDiagnosticCode: 7522 (38 CFR § 4.115b; 0% schedular absent deformity, SMC-K eligible)
primaryCondition: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) treated with SSRIs
etiologicalMechanism: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors increase synaptic serotonin, dampening dopaminergic and noradrenergic outflow in mesolimbic reward circuits and spinal centers governing erection and ejaculation; 5-HT2A/2C and 5-HT3 receptor activation contributes to reduced libido, delayed ejaculation, and impaired erectile rigidity, and serotonergic modulation of peripheral nitric-oxide signaling in cavernosal smooth muscle contributes to erectile difficulty. The effect is class-wide but agent- and dose-dependent, typically appears after treatment initiation, and often attenuates after dose reduction, discontinuation, or switch — though persistent post-SSRI sexual dysfunction is recognized. A meta-analysis restricted to studies using direct inquiry or validated questionnaires found significantly higher treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction versus placebo, ranking sertraline, venlafaxine, citalopram, paroxetine, and fluoxetine among the highest. A consecutive series of 2,040 men with sexual dysfunction found SSRI use associated with twofold risk of hypoactive desire and greater impairment of reported erectile function, with a sevenfold risk of delayed ejaculation but no difference in penile blood flow — suggesting a central/neuromodulatory rather than vascular mechanism. A FAERS pharmacovigilance analysis of 6,631,746 reports found ED the most commonly reported male sexual adverse event, with significant disproportionality signals for sertraline (ROR 6.11), citalopram (7.70), escitalopram (7.93), fluoxetine (4.97), and paroxetine (3.99); fluvoxamine's signal was not significant. Counterweights are material: a 2026 PRISMA review concluded reported ED incidence was low (<2%) and that evidence for a strong SSRI-ED link was insufficient; and untreated depression itself impairs sexual function, so baseline dysfunction must be distinguished from treatment-emergent dysfunction. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), the treatment-mediated route is legally coherent — the corpus models disorder→ED as DIRECT_CAUSATION and PTSD→ED as AGGRAVATION, both with IATROGENIC_TREATMENT_EFFECT consensus. A nexus opinion needs baseline sexual function documentation, agent/dose/timing, and exclusion of vascular, endocrine, neurologic, medication, and relationship/psychiatric causes. DC 7522 carries a 0% schedular rating unless penile deformity is present but establishes eligibility for SMC-K (loss of a creative organ).

medicalEvidence.title: Treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction related to antidepressants: a meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Serretti A, Chiesa A
medicalEvidence.summary: Meta-analysis restricted to studies that purposely investigated sexual functioning via direct inquiry or validated questionnaires: significantly higher rates of total and phase-specific treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction versus placebo, with sertraline, venlafaxine, citalopram, paroxetine, and fluoxetine showing the largest effects.

medicalEvidence.title: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor-induced sexual dysfunction
medicalEvidence.authors: Corona G, Ricca V, Bandini E, et al.
medicalEvidence.summary: Cross-sectional study of 2,040 men with sexual dysfunction: SSRI use associated with twofold risk of hypoactive sexual desire and greater impairment of reported erectile function, plus sevenfold risk of delayed ejaculation, with no difference in penile blood flow — implicating central neuromodulatory mechanisms.

medicalEvidence.title: Male sexual dysfunction associated with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs): A pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis of FAERS data
medicalEvidence.authors: Li S, Feng J, Zhang S
medicalEvidence.summary: Disproportionality analysis of 6,631,746 FAERS reports (2004 Q1-2025 Q1): erectile dysfunction was the most commonly reported male sexual adverse event; significant signals for sertraline (ROR 6.11; 5.53-6.75), citalopram (7.70), escitalopram (7.93), fluoxetine (4.97), paroxetine (3.99); fluvoxamine not significant.

medicalEvidence.title: Development of erectile dysfunction in men treated for major depressive disorder with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: a systematic review
medicalEvidence.authors: Alhuwaydi AM
medicalEvidence.summary: PRISMA systematic review of 10 studies: treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction, particularly ED, was observed in male SSRI users, but reported ED incidence was low (<2%) and the authors concluded evidence for a strong SSRI-ED link was insufficient — a key counterweight requiring case-specific evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Depression and sexual dysfunction
medicalEvidence.authors: Baldwin DS
medicalEvidence.summary: Review establishing that depression itself is associated with impaired sexual function and satisfaction even in untreated patients, and that reliable detection of treatment-emergent dysfunction requires systematic inquiry before and during treatment — the baseline-confound authority for SSRI-ED claims.
